title: Articles a, an and the
objectives: Choose a or an using the following sound.
Use the to refer to an identifiable person or thing.
Recognise common general uses without an article.

explanation.heading: Meaning and use
paragraphs: Articles are small words that come before nouns. English has the indefinite articles a and an, and the definite article the. We often use a or an when we mention one countable thing for the first time: ‘I saw a dog’. We can then use the when we talk about the same dog: ‘The dog was friendly’. The helps the listener identify the thing we mean.

Use a or an with a singular countable noun, such as a book or an apple. Use the with singular or plural nouns and with uncountable nouns when the listener can identify the thing or things: ‘the book on the table’, ‘the books on the table’ and ‘the water in this bottle’.

explanation.heading: Form
paragraphs: Choose a or an by the sound at the beginning of the next word, not simply by its first letter. Use a before a consonant sound: a teacher, a useful book. Useful begins with a ‘y’ sound. Use an before a vowel sound: an orange, an hour. The h in hour is silent for most speakers.

A singular countable noun normally needs a determiner such as an article, this or my. Say ‘She is a teacher’, not ‘She is teacher’. When the following noun begins with an adjective, choose a or an using the adjective’s first sound: ‘an old house’, but ‘a small house’.

explanation.heading: Examples in context
paragraphs: Read the examples as parts of conversations. ‘There is a café near here’ introduces a café. ‘The café closes at six’ points back to the café just mentioned. The can also identify something because of its situation: ‘Please close the door’ is natural when the speaker and listener know which door is meant.

We also use the for things understood as unique in the relevant context: ‘the sun’ and ‘the moon’. We do not normally put an article before plural or uncountable nouns when making a general statement: ‘Dogs need exercise’ and ‘Water is important’. This is a useful beginning pattern; article use has further details.

explanation.heading: Contrasts and common mistakes
paragraphs: Compare ‘I need a pen’ with ‘I need the pen on your desk’. In the first sentence, any suitable pen may be enough. In the second, the phrase identifies a particular pen. The choice depends on shared context, so a noun does not always take the same article.

Do not use a or an directly with plural nouns or uncountable nouns: say ‘a chair’ but ‘chairs’, and ‘some information’ rather than ‘an information’. Some fixed expressions and names have their own article patterns. In this unit, choose the article using the context provided rather than memorising one article for every noun.

examples.sentence: I saw a cat in the garden.
examples.note: A introduces one cat for the first time.
The refers back to the cat already mentioned.
Use an before the vowel sound at the start of engineer.
University begins with a consonant ‘y’ sound.
Hour begins with a vowel sound because its h is silent.

examples.note: The plural noun cats refers to cats generally without an article.
